title: Single-atom billiards in an ultracold bath with energy-tunable collisions and threshold-sensitive detection
authors: Silvia Hiebel, Sabrina Burgardt, Julian Feß, Artur Widera
abstract: Transport processes at the microscopic scale can differ strongly from their macroscopic counterparts, particularly when the environment is not a well-defined surface but an unordered thermal medium. Ultracold quantum gases offer a high degree of controllability and directly observable dynamics, thereby providing a versatile platform to study such transport processes under precisely controllable conditions. Here, we realize an energy-tunable single-atom collider by transporting individual cesium atoms at controlled velocity through an ultracold rubidium bath. The constant lattice velocity sets the directed contribution to the collision-energy distribution, while the lattice depth provides a tunable energy threshold for collision-induced transport disruption. By independently varying these parameters together with bath density and temperature, we separate the number of collision events from their probability to disrupt transport. Across a regime with only a few expected collisions per passage, the inferred single-collision ejection probability rises from small values to near unity as the collision energy exceeds the lattice confinement scale. The experiment thus converts microscopic collisional energy transfer into a binary single-atom observable and provides a controlled link between individual scattering events and emergent dissipative transport.
summary: This experiment uses ultracold atoms to create an energy-tunable single-atom collider, sending Cesium atoms through a Rubidium bath within an optical lattice. By precisely controlling the collision energy relative to the lattice confinement, the researchers demonstrate that transport disruption is governed by individual, discrete scattering events rather than continuous drag forces. This offers a controlled link between microscopic scattering physics and emergent dissipative transport.
main_problem: The study investigates transport processes at the microscopic scale, particularly when the environment is an unordered thermal medium, where individual scattering events dictate the outcome.
main_result: The experiment successfully converts microscopic collisional energy transfer into a binary single-atom observable, showing that the ejection probability rises sharply as collision energy exceeds the lattice confinement scale.
method: The researchers use an energy-tunable single-atom collider by transporting individual Cesium atoms through an ultracold Rubidium bath, measuring transport efficiency.
model_or_system: The system involves transporting single Cs atoms in a shallow 1D optical lattice through a controlled Rb bath. The lattice depth and constant velocity are used to tune the collision energy and set an energy threshold for transport disruption.
key_observables: Transport efficiency ($\eta_t$), single-collision ejection probability ($\langle p_{	ext{ej}} angle$), and mean free path ($\ell$).
important_parameters: Lattice depth ($U_{	ext{lat}}$), bath density ($n_{	ext{Rb}}$), bath temperature ($T$), and the ratio of collision energy to lattice confinement scale ($\langle E_{	ext{coll}} angle / U_{	ext{lat}}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the ability to independently control the collision event number and collision energy, and that the transport is governed by few, discrete collisions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup, histograms of atom positions, and plots showing transport efficiency ($\eta_t$) dependence on lattice depth and collision energy ratios, alongside calculations of the mean free path ($\ell$).
paper_structure: The paper details the experimental setup, measures transport efficiency by varying bath parameters, and then focuses on analyzing the single-collision ejection probability by tuning the collision energy relative to the lattice confinement energy.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly controllable, quantum-mechanical platform to study non-equilibrium transport and dissipation, directly linking single-particle scattering events to macroscopic transport properties, which is crucial for understanding open quantum systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Experimental setup and data evaluation. a) Sketch of the experimental setup. The Rb cloud and the individual Cs atoms are initially prepared in spatially separated regions. Both species are confined radially by a common dipole-trap beam propagating along the z direction. Following the preparation stage, the Cs atoms are loaded into a one-dimensional optical lattice, which enables their controlled transport along the shared dipole trap into or beyond the Rb cloud. b) Exemplary histogram showing the summed Cs atom positions along the z direction for 12 individual measurement runs. The colored vertical lines indicate the centers of the corresponding regions: green line: Cs preparation...

FIG. 2: Cs atom transport in the one-dimensional lattice. a) Lattice motion during transport. The purple graph shows the acceleration during transport, the teal graph shows the velocity, and the light green curve shows the corresponding distance traveled. The orange background indicates when the atoms traverse the Rb bath. b) Transport efficiency of the Cs atoms without additional Rb bath as a function of lattice depth and acceleration. The black dashed line indicates Ulat/kB = sa, with s = 5 × 10−3 µK s2 m−1 and shows the boundary between locked and running behavior.

FIG. 3: Transport efficiency for different bath parameters. a) Low-density: T = 955 ± 16 nK, n = 0.60 ± 0.07 × 1013 cm−3. b) Intermediate-density: T = 918 ± 40 nK, n = 1.55 ± 0.06 × 1013 cm−3. c) High-density: T = 906 ± 40 nK, n = 1.80 ± 0.05 × 1013 cm−3. The displayed results are averages over 15 repetitions for each data point. d) Integrated transport efficiency relative to the efficiency without the Rb bath. The labels indicate the assignment of panels a)-c). e) Maximum average number of collisions for different bath parameters at a velocity of 7 cm s−1. Each column shows results for one lattice velocity, while the rows represent two different lattice depths (given in units of temperature). The column density is reduced as the lattice depth increases. For a lattice depth of Ulat/kB = 38 µK, the cloud densities are visibly reduced, and their profile is elongated in the z-direction.
